doc.title: Lou Donaldson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: How his records differed from club sets
summary: He tested tunes in clubs before recording them and changed personnel as needed.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Again, talking about the band, do the Blue Note recordings from 1957-1958-1959, like Blues Walk or Sunny Side Up reflect what your band was playing in those clubs?
No. Because I used all that on those things... I wasn’t even playing organ in those clubs.
On Sunny Side Up you used piano. Horace Parlan.
Oh, ok. Maybe I did. I went on the road with that group, Horace Parlan, George Tucker and Al Harewood, and I had Tommy Turrentine on trumpet.
So the records were not a direct reflection of what you would do in the club.

Well, when they wanted a date, I’d just figure out something to do to make it. I’d change the personnel according to what I was playing at that time. What I used to do, I used to play... If I was going to make a date, two weeks before I made it, I’d play the tunes in the club to see what kind of response I got, and the ones I didn’t get a response to, I didn’t record, and I was home free. Because everything I made during that time, sold.
Probably a lot of ‘78s also at that time.
